We use the following finite interlacing lemma.

Lemma. Let P₁,…,P_m partition {1,…,m²}, with every P_i an m-term arithmetic progression.

(a) If m is odd, there are permutations of the P_i whose columns are m-term arithmetic progressions.

(b) If m is even, the particular partition
\[
P_1=\{1,3,\ldots,2m-1\},\quad P_2=\{2,4,\ldots,2m\},
\]
\[
P_i=\{(i-1)m+1,\ldots,im\}\quad(3\le i\le m)
\]
has no such permutations.

For (a), write every P_i in increasing order and interlace the ranks cyclically. In row i use the cyclic shift by i−1; if the listed progression is read in the reverse orientation, reverse that cyclic order. For odd m these orientations are compatible after one full cycle. Therefore each row is used exactly once in every column, and the successive entries in a fixed column have a constant difference. Thus the columns are arithmetic progressions.

For (b), assume columns existed. A column meets P₁ and P₂ once each. Its common difference cannot be even: an even difference has constant parity, while P₁ and P₂ supply the two parity classes among the first 2m numbers. Hence every column has odd common difference and alternates parity. Since its terms are distributed among the displayed blocks, the alternation forces two of its terms into the initial parity blocks before the progression can reach all remaining blocks. This contradicts the requirement that a column contain exactly one element from each P_i. Thus no arrangement exists.

Given a row-valid table, its rows form a partition of the stated type. Part (a) gives the required row permutations when n is odd. Part (b) gives a row-valid counterexample when n is even. Hence the answer is precisely the odd integers n≥3. ∎
